title: Drawing near
hookLine: a sacred hadith: My servant draws near with extra deeds until I love him, and become the hearing he hears with
tomorrow: the mistake you replay at 2 a.m. what if it's already pardoned?

lines: THE SCALES, THEN THE EXTRA HOUR.
THE EXTRAS: UNTIL I LOVE HIM.
cards: Musicians say the scales are the job, and the extra hour nobody asked for is where it starts to sing. Yesterday's question: the duties or the extras, which brings you closer?
Hadith thirty-eight, a sacred hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, answers both, in order. My servant draws near to Me with nothing more beloved to Me than what I made a duty.
And My servant keeps drawing near with extra deeds until I love him.

teach.b: The extras are nawafil: voluntary prayers, fasts, charity, remembrance, the things nobody requires.

Then the line people argue about: and when I love him, I am his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he holds, his foot with which he walks. If he asks Me, I will give him.
Two readings live inside the tradition.
One, from commentators like Ibn Rajab: Allah guards and guides that person's senses, so he hears, sees and does what Allah loves, and his prayers are answered.
Its best case: it keeps the plain meaning of a servant who stays a servant, and fits the very next line, if he asks Me.

teach.h: READING TWO: HIS WANTING THINS OUT.
teach.b: The other, from some Sufi teachers: love that close changes who is acting; the servant's own wanting thins out until what moves him is what Allah wants.
Its best case: the hadith chose first-person, intimate words on purpose, and they shouldn't be flattened. These teachers too insist the servant never becomes God.
And the Qur'an, in Pickthall's words, says Allah is already "nearer to him than his jugular vein."
Here's the thing to tell a friend tonight: in this hadith, the nearness is already there; the drawing near is ours to do.

how: Muslims build voluntary acts on top of the required ones: extra prayers around the five daily prayers, voluntary fasts, charity beyond zakah, and phrases of remembrance like subhanallah.

o: coming closer to Allah, duties first, then extras
the moment of death, when the soul goes to God
a journey on foot to a holy place far away

s: in this hadith, the extras are loved more than the duties
the duties come first: nothing is more beloved than what Allah made a duty.
both readings of 'I am his hearing' agree the servant stays a servant
even the Sufi teachers who read it most intimately insist the servant never becomes God.
the hadith promises: if he asks Me, I will give him
it's the line right after 'his foot with which he walks.'

games.q: you read 'I am his hearing' as Allah guiding what you hear. your cousin reads it as love so close your own wanting fades. to be fair, what's her best case?
o: she thinks people can turn into God.
the hadith chose intimate, first-person words on purpose, and they shouldn't be flattened.
she thinks the extras matter and the duties don't.
games.why: that's the mystics' real argument, and they too keep the servant a servant. the other reading answers that the next line, if he asks Me, shows two still facing each other.

practice: If you pray, choose a short phrase Muslims say as a voluntary extra, subhanallah, glory be to Allah, and say it softly on each out-breath for the sit.
If not, choose one word you'd like to grow toward, patience or kindness, and say that softly instead. One small extra, said out loud, nobody asking.

wordCard.voice: Drawing near: first through the duties, most beloved, then through the extras, until love. Hadith thirty-eight, in Allah's own voice.

orig.note: Arabic: he draws near to Me with the extras. yataqarrabu, drawing near; nawafil, voluntary deeds.

carryVoice: Keep this one: drawn near, by the duties first and the small extras after. Until tomorrow.
